t: LeetCode 1810 - Minimum Path Cost in a Hidden Grid: Explore Blind, Then Dijkstra
o: The grid is hidden: dimensions, blocked cells, costs, even the robot position are unknown and can only be probed through GridMaster queries. Every entered cell charges its own cost and all costs are positive, so finding the cheapest route is a single-source shortest path with positive weights, which calls for Dijkstra rather than BFS. The strategy is two-phase: first flood-fill the reachable component by DFS, physically moving into every open neighbor and immediately moving back afterwards, recording each discovered relative coordinate together with the entry cost move() returned and noting the target coordinates whenever isTarget() fires. With the weighted map reconstructed, run Dijkstra from the start over known cells only; in example 1 the probes reveal costs 2, 1 and 1 around the start and Dijkstra answers 2. If exploration never sees the target, the component is disconnected and the answer is -1.
k: Interactive grids are usually solved in two phases: reconstruct the map with DFS backtracking moves, then run a graph algorithm on what you drew.
move() pays the ENTRY cost of the destination cell, so edge weights differ and Dijkstra beats BFS.
After every exploratory move you must move the robot back; forgetting this corrupts every later query.

a.i: Walk the component recursively: for each direction that canMove allows toward an unvisited relative coordinate, move, store the returned cost at that coordinate, recurse, then move back in the opposite direction. Record target coordinates whenever isTarget() holds. Afterwards run standard lazy-deletion Dijkstra from (0,0), relaxing only neighbors present in the discovered map, and return the distance the first time the target pops off the heap.
s: DFS from the start storing cost[(x,y)] per discovered relative cell; note the target when isTarget() fires
If the target was never seen, return -1
Dijkstra with a min-heap: entering neighbor (nx,ny) costs d + cost[(nx,ny)]
Return the popped distance the first time the target settles
a.t: O(mn log(mn)) - the DFS touches each reachable cell once and the heap adds a logarithmic factor.
a.sp: O(mn) - discovered-cost map, distances, recursion stack and heap.

a.n: Approach 2: DFS Mapping + Dial Bucket Queue
a.i: Cell costs lie between 1 and 100 and at most 100 x 100 cells exist, so no path cost exceeds about one million. That bounded integer range makes Dial algorithm buckets attractive: one FIFO list per distance value and an outward-sweeping cursor replace the heap entirely, removing its logarithmic factor - a strong answer when the interviewer pushes on constants.
s: Map the grid exactly as in Approach 1
Place the start in bucket 0 of an array indexed by path cost
Sweep cursor d upward; settling a cell relaxes each discovered neighbor into bucket d + cost(neighbor)
Return d the first time the target settles
a.t: O(mn + C) where C <= mn x 100 is the largest swept bucket index - linear, no log factor.
a.sp: O(mn + C) for the map, distances and buckets.

w: Say the two-phase plan out loud first - map interactively, then compute shortest paths - because that framing is what gets graded. Pitfalls: forgetting to undo exploratory moves, charging the start cell (its cost never applies), marking visited by direction instead of by coordinate, and missing the -1 disconnected case. Follow-ups worth mentioning: reconstruct the actual route by keeping parent pointers during relaxation, use Dial buckets given the 1..100 cost bound, or plain BFS if every move had equal cost.
